The ${}^{1}\mathrm{H}$ -NMR spectrum $(\mathrm{CDCl}_3)$ exhibits a singlet at $\delta = 7.16$ for the $\mathrm{NH}_2$ protons, in addition to multiplets for the $\mathrm{NCH}_3$ , $\mathrm{CH}_2$ (2 quartets), and $\mathrm{CCH}_3$ groups.
X-ray structure analysis of 1 (cf. Fig. 1) indicated that the central molybdenum atom has a distorted pentagonal-bipyramidal coordination.

To visualize this geometry, imagine a pentagonal prism where the top and bottom faces are capped; in this specific case, the "equator" is a five-membered ring, and the "poles" are the axial positions.

The chelate ring of the hydrazido(1−) ligand lies in the equatorial plane, together with three of the four sulfur atoms of the two Me₂NCS₂ ligands; the remaining sulfur atom and the diazenido ligand occupy the two apices of the coordination polyhedron.
This arrangement is crucial because the specific placement of ligands dictates the electronic environment of the metal center.
The Mo-diazenido group is almost linear (Mo-N1-N2:178(1)°);
this near-perfect linearity is a hallmark of strong multiple bonding, similar to how a taut string resists bending. The
distances Mo-N1 (177(1) pm) and N1-N2 (121(1) pm) suggest multiple bonding and considerable electron delocalization;
electrons are not stuck between just two atoms but are shared across the Mo-N-N framework, strengthening the connection. The
distance N2-C is 136(1) pm and the angle N1-N2-C 120(1)°. The framework atoms of the diazenido ligand and those of the hydrazido ligand lie in a plane.
This planar alignment allows for optimal orbital overlap, facilitating the delocalization mentioned earlier.

The N−N distance in the chelate ring of the latter is 145(1) pm, the C−N distance of 123(1) pm corresponds to the formulation as a double bond, and the Mo−N distance (amino group) of 225.0(8) to a normal coordinative bond[4].

Here, the bond lengths act as a diagnostic tool: shorter distances imply stronger, double-bond character, while the longer Mo-N distance indicates a standard dative bond where the nitrogen lone pair is simply donated to the metal.
The Mo−S distances in the equatorial plane vary between 246.4(4) and 252.6(4) pm; Mo−Sax is longer (256.2(4) pm) due to the trans-effect of N1.

The "trans-effect" is a powerful concept in coordination chemistry: a strong ligand (like the diazenido group) sitting directly opposite (trans to) another ligand weakens the bond of that opposite ligand. Think of it as a tug-of-war where the strong pull of the N1 ligand stretches the bond to the sulfur atom on the other side, making it longer and weaker.
Our structural investigation indicates that different substituents on N2 decisively influence the bonding relationship in the diazenido group and, hence, the reactivity of the nitrogen atoms.
This is a critical insight: by changing the "tail" of the molecule (the substituent), we can tune the "head" (the reactive nitrogen center).

Thus, the Mo-N1 and N1-N2 distances in the diazenido complex $[Mo\{Me_{2}NCS_{2}\}_{3}[N_{2}C(O)OEt]$ with the electronegative ethoxycarbonyl substituent are 173.2(5) and 127.4(7) pm, respectively $^{[5]}$ .

Notice how the introduction of the electronegative ethoxycarbonyl group pulls electron density away, shortening the Mo-N1 bond and lengthening the N1-N2 bond compared to our previous example, effectively altering the molecule's reactivity profile.

By Roberta Bertani, Giovanni Carturan\*, and Alberto Scrivanti
We previously observed that $[(η^{3}-C_{3}H_{5})Pt(L)H]$ 2 is stable in toluene between -80 and $-30^{\circ}C$ , but decomposes with evolution of propene above $-20^{\circ}C^{[3]}$ . This represents the collapse of the 14-electron $Pt^{0}$ intermediate 3, the occurrence of which has been demonstrated by variable temperature NMR spectroscopy.

To understand this, recall that transition metals often seek a stable 18-electron configuration. Complex 2 is stable at low temperatures, but as it warms up, it loses a ligand to form a highly reactive, electron-deficient 14-electron species (Complex 3). This intermediate is fleeting and unstable, quickly breaking down to release propene gas.

Unexpected Ring-Opening of Benzocyclobutenes upon Reaction with Lithium in Tetrahydrofuran
By Adalbert Maercker\*, Willi Berkulin, and Peter Schiess
Although the conrotatory ring-opening of the benzocyclobutene radical anion is thermally allowed, previously reported results were revoked shortly after their publication $^{[1]}$ .
We have found a completely different reaction path—scission of a $C_{aryl}-CH_{2}$ bond—in the reaction of benzocyclobutene (1,2-dihydrocyclobutabenzene) $^{[**]}$ 1 $^{[2]}$ with lithium powder in tetrahydrofuran (THF). The expected o-xylene was not detected, even in trace amounts. Instead, after hydrolysis ethylbenzene 9 and its subsequent product 8, which may have been formed via the dilithio compound 6, was obtained (Scheme 1; the relative yields were determined by gas chromatography: after four weeks at room temperature conversion was only 20%).
